dominantMode: Historical argument + source analysis + historiographical interpretation
cleanRule: Modern History = construct an historical argument + analyse and interpret sources (written, visual, official, personal) + evaluate differing historical interpretations + use historical concepts (causation, continuity and change, perspectives, significance, contestability)
leaderboardTip: HSC Modern History rewards specific historical evidence — named events with dates (Enabling Act March 1933, Tet Offensive January 1968), named individuals (Goebbels, Gorbachev, Deng Xiaoping), named sources and named historians (Kershaw, Fitzpatrick, Dower, Gaddis). Generic statements about 'the government' or 'the people' without specific evidence cannot reach Band 5. Always link evidence to the historical argument.

examStructure.sectionI: Source-based questions on the Core Study (Power and Authority in the Modern World 1919–1946): analysis, interpretation and evaluation of provided sources, including short answers and a longer source-based response — 25 marks
examStructure.sectionII: Extended response (essay) on ONE National Studies topic — school options: Japan 1904–1937, Australia 1918–1949, Russia and the Soviet Union 1917–1941, USA 1919–1941 — 25 marks
examStructure.sectionIII: Extended response (essay) on ONE Peace and Conflict topic — school options: Conflict in Indochina 1954–1979, Conflict in the Pacific 1937–1951, Conflict in Europe 1935–1945, The Cold War 1945–1991 — 25 marks
examStructure.sectionIV: Extended response (essay) on ONE Change in the Modern World topic — school options: The Cultural Revolution to Tiananmen Square 1966–1989, Civil Rights in the USA 1945–1968, The Changing World Order 1945–2011, The Nuclear Age 1945–2011, Apartheid in South Africa 1960–1994 — 25 marks

coreStudy.title: Core Study: Power and Authority in the Modern World 1919–1946
coreStudy.contentFocus: Through a focus on the nature of power and authority 1919–1946, and a broader transnational perspective, students investigate the rise of fascist, totalitarian and militarist movements after World War I; what drew people to these movements; the regimes that emerged and ongoing international efforts to achieve collective security. Through a study of Germany as a key example, students develop an understanding of how a democracy can collapse, the impact of dictatorship on a society, the elimination of individual freedoms, and the threats that dictatorships can pose to peace and security.

dotPoints: An overview of the peace treaties which ended World War I and their consequences

dotPoints: The conditions that enabled dictators to rise to power in the interwar period

sourceAnalysis.description: Explaining the meaning and value of sources for historical inquiry; analysing sources for different perspectives; analysing and synthesising evidence from different source types; identifying problems relating to sources. In Section I, students analyse, interpret and evaluate PROVIDED sources on the Core Study.
keyQuestions: What type of source is it (official document, speech, propaganda, photograph, cartoon, memoir, historian's account)?
Who created it, when, and for what purpose and audience?
What does it reveal about the topic — and what perspective does it present?
What are its limitations and biases (propaganda purpose, hindsight, self-justification, censorship)?
How does it compare or corroborate with other available sources?
How useful and reliable is this source for a historian studying the topic?

Band6.descriptor: Demonstrates extensive knowledge and understanding of a range of historical features, people, places, events and developments, and their significance. Demonstrates comprehensive understanding of continuity and change over time. Demonstrates comprehensive understanding of different perspectives of individuals and groups in the past. Analyses and interprets sources for evidence and synthesises evidence. Evaluates differing interpretations and representations of the past. Demonstrates sophisticated understanding and use of historical concepts and terms. Communicates a high level and sustained argument through well-structured and comprehensive texts.
keyFeatures: Extensive knowledge across historical features, people, places, events and developments
Comprehensive understanding of continuity and change
Analyses AND interprets sources for evidence — AND synthesises evidence across sources
Sophisticated understanding and use of historical concepts and terms
High level, SUSTAINED argument through well-structured and COMPREHENSIVE texts

Band5.descriptor: Demonstrates thorough knowledge and understanding of a range of historical features, people, places, events and developments, and their significance. Demonstrates a well-developed understanding of continuity and change over time. Demonstrates a well-developed understanding of different perspectives of individuals and groups in the past. Analyses and interprets sources for evidence. Analyses differing interpretations and representations of the past. Demonstrates thorough understanding and use of historical concepts and terms. Communicates a coherent and sustained argument through well-structured and comprehensive texts.
keyFeatures: Thorough knowledge of historical features, people, places, events and developments
Well-developed understanding of continuity and change
Analyses and interprets sources for evidence (synthesises at Band 6 — analyses at Band 5)
Thorough understanding and use of historical concepts and terms
Coherent and sustained argument through well-structured and comprehensive texts

Band4.descriptor: Demonstrates sound knowledge and understanding of a range of historical features, people, places, events and developments, and their significance. Demonstrates sound understanding of continuity and change over time. Demonstrates sound understanding of different perspectives of individuals and groups in the past. Uses sources for evidence. Discusses interpretations and representations of the past. Demonstrates understanding of historical concepts and terms. Communicates a general argument through well-structured texts.
keyFeatures: Sound knowledge of historical features, people, places, events and developments
Sound understanding of continuity and change
USES sources for evidence (analyses at Band 5)
Understanding of historical concepts and terms

Band3.descriptor: Demonstrates basic understanding of historical features, people, places, events, and their significance. Identifies features of continuity and change over time. Demonstrates basic understanding of different perspectives of individuals and groups in the past. Makes reference to sources. Identifies interpretations and representations of the past. Uses basic historical concepts and terms. Communicates basic information through descriptive texts.
keyFeatures: Makes reference to sources (uses at Band 4)

Band2.descriptor: Describes historical features, people, places and events. Recognises aspects of continuity and/or change. Demonstrates limited understanding of different perspectives of individuals and groups in the past. Makes reference to sources. Uses limited historical concepts and terms. Provides limited information in narrative style.

Band1.descriptor: Performance reported as Band 1 indicates that the minimum standard expected was not demonstrated.

dominant_question_types: Section I (Core): assess the usefulness and/or reliability of provided sources for a historian studying power and authority 1919–1946
Section I (Core): use the source(s) AND own knowledge to explain or account for a feature of the period (e.g. Nazi consolidation of power, methods of control)
Assess/evaluate the significance of an individual, event or development (e.g. the role of Emperor Hirohito, the significance of the Tet Offensive)
To what extent... (e.g. To what extent was the New Deal successful? To what extent was Gorbachev responsible for the end of the Cold War?)
Account for the rise/collapse of... (e.g. account for the rise of militarism in Japan, account for the collapse of apartheid)
Analyse the impact of the conflict/regime/movement on civilians or specific groups
Evaluate differing historical interpretations of a key debate (e.g. the decision to drop the A-bomb, the origins of the Cold War)
modern_history_specific_tips: ALWAYS anchor claims to specific evidence — named events with dates (Enabling Act March 1933, Sharpeville March 1960), named individuals, named legislation, statistics where relevant. Generic references to 'the government' or 'the war' earn Band 3 at best.

For Section I: address BOTH usefulness AND reliability where asked — usefulness is about what the source offers a historian for a specific inquiry; reliability is about accuracy, perspective, purpose and provenance. A biased propaganda source can still be highly USEFUL for studying propaganda.
For Section I: always integrate 'own knowledge' with the source content when the question asks for it — quoting or describing the source alone caps the mark.

Include historiography in essays — name historians (Kershaw, Fitzpatrick, Gaddis, Dower, Dikötter) and their interpretations, especially where they differ. Evaluating competing interpretations distinguishes Band 6 from Band 5.
Use historical concepts explicitly — frame arguments around causation, continuity and change, perspectives, significance and contestability. Don't just narrate events chronologically.
Stay inside the topic's date range — evidence outside the prescribed period (e.g. post-1937 Japan in the National Study, post-1941 USSR) earns no credit.
For 'account for' and 'to what extent' questions: weigh multiple factors, rank their relative importance, and make an explicit judgement — not just a list of causes.
common_errors: Narrating events chronologically without constructing an argument ('First Hitler became Chancellor, then...' without evaluating causation or significance).
Confusing usefulness with reliability in Section I source questions, or asserting a source is 'biased so unreliable' without analysing purpose and audience.
Describing sources without linking them to the question's specific inquiry focus.
Ignoring historiography — not naming any historians or their interpretations in extended responses.
Describing both sides of a debate without making a judgement — Band 5-6 requires evaluation, not just discussion.
Straying outside the prescribed date range of the topic (e.g. discussing Pearl Harbor in Japan 1904–1937, or post-1968 events in Civil Rights 1945–1968).
Using general terms ('the people', 'the government', 'sources show') without specific names, dates and evidence.

argument_construction_steps: State a clear historical thesis or argument in response to the question.
Identify the historical period, context, and relevant aspects of the prescribed topic.
Present specific evidence — named events, dates, individuals, legislation, statistics — to support the argument.
Where sources are provided (Section I), analyse and evaluate them: what do they reveal, and what are their limitations?
Integrate at least one historical interpretation (named historian) and assess it in extended responses.
Apply historical concepts: causation, continuity and change, significance, perspectives, contestability.
Conclude with a judgement that directly answers the question.
source_analysis_steps: Identify the source type (official document, speech, propaganda poster, photograph, cartoon, memoir, historian's account).
Identify the creator, date, purpose and intended audience.
State what the source reveals about the topic (its usefulness for the historian's specific inquiry).
Assess reliability: perspective, purpose, propaganda value, hindsight, self-justification, censorship.
Comment on what the source does NOT reveal or may misrepresent (limitations).
Cross-reference with other sources and own knowledge where possible.
Link the source analysis to the historical argument or inquiry question.

before_output: Is a clear historical argument stated and sustained?
Is specific evidence cited — named events, dates, individuals, legislation?
Where sources are involved, are they evaluated (usefulness AND reliability/limitations)?
Is historiography included in extended responses (named historian and their view)?
Are historical concepts used explicitly (causation, significance, continuity/change, perspectives)?
Does the response address perspectives (individual, group, national, ideological)?
Is all evidence inside the prescribed topic and date range?
Does the conclusion directly address the question with a judgement?
band6_checklist: Extensive, specific historical knowledge across multiple aspects of the topic.
Comprehensive understanding of continuity and change — both identified and assessed.
Sources analysed, interpreted AND synthesised (with own knowledge in Section I).
Differing historical interpretations EVALUATED — not just described.
Sophisticated use of historical concepts and terminology throughout.
High-level sustained argument — not a narrative or list of facts.
Comprehensive texts — detailed, well-structured, covering the breadth of the question.

target_band_selection_rule.Band6: Extensive knowledge, comprehensive continuity/change analysis, synthesis of sources with own knowledge, evaluation of differing historiographical interpretations, sophisticated historical concepts, sustained high-level argument.
target_band_selection_rule.Band5: Thorough knowledge, well-developed continuity/change, analysis and interpretation of sources, analysis of interpretations (not full evaluation), thorough historical concepts, coherent sustained argument.
target_band_selection_rule.Band4: Sound knowledge, sound continuity/change, uses sources for evidence (references without deep analysis), discusses interpretations, understands historical concepts, general argument.
target_band_selection_rule.Band3: Basic knowledge, identifies continuity/change, makes reference to sources, identifies interpretations, basic terms, descriptive text.
target_band_selection_rule.Band2: Describes events, recognises change, limited terms, narrative style.
target_band_selection_rule.Band1: Do not generate unless explicitly requested.

forbidden_behaviours: Do not construct a response that only narrates events without building an historical argument.
Do not use generic evidence references — always name specific events, dates, individuals and legislation.
Do not ignore historiography in extended responses — always include at least one named historian.
Do not describe interpretations without evaluating them at Band 5-6.
Do not confuse the topic period — all evidence must sit inside the prescribed date range of the option being answered.
Do not mark a response against the wrong option — confirm which National Studies / Peace and Conflict / Change in the Modern World option the question belongs to before marking.

modernHistoryNote: Modern History CUBE marking has important differences from Science subjects and from Ancient History. The Underline step should identify: named individuals (Hitler, Stalin, Mandela, Deng Xiaoping), named events with dates (Enabling Act 1933, Tet Offensive 1968, Sharpeville 1960), named legislation and treaties, named source types (propaganda posters, cartoons, speeches, official documents, memoirs), named historical concepts (causation, continuity and change, significance, perspectives, contestability), and any directive verbs that trigger source evaluation or historiographical judgement. Section I questions come with PROVIDED sources — the Evaluate/plan step must show how each source will be used AND supplemented with own knowledge. Planning arrows should show: thesis → evidence (named events/individuals/dates) → source analysis (usefulness/reliability where relevant) → historiography (named historian) → judgement. Before marking, confirm which topic option the question belongs to — this subject spans one core plus thirteen school-taught options across three elective sections, each with its own prescribed date range.
